title: Load balancing
simple: One address receives requests and shares them across healthy copies of your application. It chooses a destination; it does not create extra servers or make slow database queries disappear.
analogy: A school has three lunch counters. A helper sends each child to an open counter instead of letting everyone crowd around the first. If a counter closes, the helper stops using it. But if all counters share one empty kitchen, the helper cannot create food. Likewise, distributing requests does not remove a shared database bottleneck.
why: In our fictional SeatSpot ticket app, many people open the same event at once. One application instance becomes overloaded while a second has spare capacity. A load balancer makes the spare capacity reachable through the same public endpoint.
engineering: At layer 4, routing works with transport connections; at layer 7 it can inspect HTTP paths, hosts or headers. Pick based on protocol, routing needs and operational cost rather than assuming layer 7 is always better.

Round robin distributes turns, not equal processing time. Least-connections can help with different connection lifetimes; weights can reflect unequal capacity. Health/readiness checks must represent whether a target can actually serve traffic.

Keep login/session state outside individual application memory when requests may reach different replicas. Drain old connections during removal. Retries of booking/payment requests need idempotency keys so a lost response does not create a second purchase.

worked.scenario: Suppose one tested replica handles 200 requests/second within the latency objective and the expected peak is 450.
worked.calculation: Three replicas provide 600 requests/second in the simplified model. Losing one leaves 400, below the peak. Four leave 600 after one failure. Real capacity must be load-tested with the database and dependencies.
worked.decision: Use four if that failure headroom is required and affordable. Monitor per-target latency, error rate and queueing; do not infer usable capacity from instance count alone.

implementation.explanation: This minimal reverse-proxy configuration shares requests between two targets. It omits production TLS, timeouts and platform-specific health checks. Run such infrastructure locally or in your own environment, not in the browser compiler.

useCases: Stateless web/API replicas behind one endpoint.
Spreading reads or connections across healthy service instances.
pitfalls: Calling round robin a guarantee of equal CPU usage.
Making the load balancer a single unprotected instance.
Retrying a purchase without an idempotency key.

exercise.prompt: You have three replicas each safe at 150 requests/second. Peak demand is 350. Can you survive one replica failing?
hints: Calculate surviving capacity, not total capacity.
Separate the mathematical estimate from measured performance.
exercise.solution: After a failure, two replicas provide 300, below 350. Four total leave 450 after one failure in this simplified model. Also test dependency limits and the actual request mix.

interview.question: How would you choose a load-balancing policy?
interview.answer: Start with request shape, connection lifetime, replica capacity and state. Use a simple policy, health checks and observed tail latency; change it when measurements show imbalance.
interview.followUp: What happens to active WebSocket connections during scale-in?

interview.question: Does a load balancer make a system highly available?
interview.answer: It is one part. The balancing tier, application replicas, data layer and failure detection all need suitable redundancy and recovery. Shared dependencies can still fail the request.
interview.followUp: Where would you look when every target is slow at once?

quiz.question: A load balancer is healthy but all database calls are slow. What should you investigate?
options: The shared database and dependency saturation
quiz.explanation: The application can share work and still wait on the same constrained dependency. Measure the request path before scaling.

steps.title: One public address
steps.detail: Visitors send event requests to one endpoint. The load balancer selects an application target so visitors do not need to know individual server addresses.

steps.title: Share requests
steps.detail: Alternate requests between App A and App B. This shares turns, but a slow request can still occupy one target much longer than another.

steps.title: A target fails
steps.detail: App A stops passing readiness checks. Detection takes time; requests already in flight may fail and must be handled safely by the client.

steps.title: Use the healthy target
steps.detail: New requests go to App B after the target is removed. App B needs enough spare capacity; routing cannot manufacture capacity during an outage.

steps.title: Protect the booking
steps.detail: Both copies use the same order system. A repeated booking request carries the same idempotency key so a lost response does not charge twice.

steps.title: Measure the whole path
steps.detail: Check latency and errors at the balancer, application and database. If both applications wait on the database, adding routing rules will not fix that bottleneck.

title: Auto scaling
simple: Auto scaling changes capacity automatically when measured demand changes. A controller observes a signal, chooses a replica count and waits for new capacity to become ready. It is a delayed feedback loop, not instant unlimited capacity.
analogy: A shop manager sees a long checkout queue and opens another counter. Opening takes time: someone must arrive, sign in and prepare the till. Closing every quiet counter immediately would cause a new queue a minute later. The manager needs minimum staffing and patience, not just a rule that reacts to every small change.
why: SeatSpot traffic grows before a popular sale. Manual scaling may arrive too late, while leaving peak capacity running all day wastes resources. Automatic control can help, provided start-up delay and dependency limits are included.
engineering: Choose a signal related to the bottleneck: CPU for CPU-bound work, queue age/backlog for asynchronous jobs, or concurrency for request workers. Low CPU does not prove health when threads are waiting on a database.

Set minimum/maximum replicas, readiness checks and scale-down stabilization. A controller can request replicas while the cluster lacks nodes or the account lacks quota. Application scaling and infrastructure scaling are different loops.

New instances can amplify database connections or cold-cache misses. Warm up carefully, bound aggregate concurrency and alert when desired capacity cannot become ready. Scheduled pre-scaling may suit a known ticket-sale time.

worked.scenario: Four replicas average 80% CPU. The target is 50%, assuming similar replicas and CPU-bound work.
worked.calculation: A simplified estimate is ceil(4 × 80 / 50) = 7 replicas. This is a teaching estimate; real controllers apply tolerances, readiness handling and other policies.
worked.decision: Check whether seven replicas can start, whether their total database connections fit, and whether latency improves. A replica recommendation is not proof the system is safe.

implementation.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: seatspot}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: seatspot}
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}
implementation.explanation: Illustrative Kubernetes configuration. CPU utilization needs CPU requests on containers and a working metrics pipeline. It does not provision a cluster or guarantee a latency objective.

useCases: Traffic with changing demand and predictable start-up characteristics.
Worker pools with measurable backlog and safe downstream concurrency.
pitfalls: Scaling on CPU while the database is the real bottleneck.
Ignoring cold starts, quotas and node capacity.
Rapid scale-down that repeatedly destroys useful warm capacity.

exercise.prompt: A queue receives 120 jobs/second. Each worker handles 20. How many workers stop backlog growth, and why might you need more?
hints: Six matches arrivals exactly.
Recovery from a backlog requires surplus throughput.
exercise.solution: Six workers match the average under ideal assumptions. More are needed to drain existing backlog and tolerate failures or variable duration, within downstream safety limits. Monitor oldest-job age, not just queue size.

interview.question: Why can autoscaling make an outage worse?
interview.answer: More replicas can open more database connections, retry unhealthy dependencies and miss the same cache. Bound concurrency and investigate the bottleneck; scale only where added capacity helps.
interview.followUp: Which metric would reveal that workers are waiting rather than computing?

interview.question: How would you avoid oscillation?
interview.answer: Use suitable sampling, minimum capacity, stabilization and controlled scale-in. Measure startup and shutdown behavior and test repeated bursts.
interview.followUp: What would you pre-scale before a scheduled launch?

quiz.question: What does adding application replicas guarantee?
options: That requested capacity immediately becomes ready
quiz.explanation: Scaling has delays and shared constraints. Observe readiness, capacity and end-to-end latency.

steps.title: Observe demand
steps.detail: The application serves visitors while metrics record utilization and request behavior. Select a signal related to the constrained resource, not simply the easiest chart.

steps.title: Choose a target
steps.detail: The controller compares the observed signal with a configured target and computes a desired replica count within minimum and maximum limits.

steps.title: Request capacity
steps.detail: The controller requests more replicas. Scheduling, image download, initialization and health checks take time. Desired capacity and ready capacity can differ.

steps.title: Wait for readiness
steps.detail: Only ready replicas should receive normal traffic. If nodes or quotas are exhausted, a controller cannot create the missing physical capacity by itself.

steps.title: Check dependencies
steps.detail: More application copies can increase database connections. Limit aggregate concurrency so solving an application bottleneck does not create a database outage.

steps.title: Scale down carefully
steps.detail: After demand falls, stabilization prevents rapid shrinking and regrowth. Drain work before removing replicas and keep enough minimum capacity for the next burst.

title: High availability
simple: High availability means meeting an agreed target for successful service over time. Redundant components and recovery reduce downtime, but a system can never promise that nothing will ever fail.
analogy: A school keeps two water pumps so one can help when the other stops. If both use the same broken power line, two pumps do not solve the problem. Availability depends on the whole chain and on how quickly people notice and recover, not just the number of pumps.
why: SeatSpot must keep ticket browsing and booking usable when a machine or zone fails. Different features can have different objectives: cached event descriptions may remain available even if booking is temporarily paused to protect correct seat allocation.
engineering: Define a user-visible service level indicator, such as the fraction of valid booking attempts that finish correctly within a latency boundary. State the measurement window and exclusions before quoting an availability percentage.

Distribute replicas across relevant failure domains, such as machines or zones, and examine shared data stores, network paths, credentials and deployment systems. Two replicas on one failed host do not survive that host failure.

Redundancy needs health detection, failover and survivor capacity. Test the complete user operation during a controlled failure. Maintenance, bad configuration and deployment errors can consume the error budget as well as hardware faults.

worked.scenario: An agreed objective is 99.9% time availability over an illustrative 30-day month.
worked.calculation: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. A 0.1% unavailability budget is 43.2 minutes. Request-based indicators use failed eligible requests instead, so do not mix the two measurements.
worked.decision: Choose the objective from business needs and recovery cost. Measure actual booking success separately from whether the homepage responds.

implementation.code:
# Fragment, not a complete Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: {app: seatspot}
implementation.explanation: This fragment illustrates spreading matching pods across zones. A working cluster, complete pod template and matching labels are required. It does not make the database multi-zone or remove all shared failure modes.

useCases: Services with explicit uptime and latency objectives.
Critical user journeys that must tolerate an infrastructure failure.
pitfalls: Equating a green server-health page with successful purchases.
Putting all redundant copies in one failure domain.
Ignoring the capacity needed after failover.

exercise.prompt: Two application replicas run in one zone. A second zone is added. List three things to verify before calling the service highly available.
hints: Follow a real booking from entry point to storage.
Ask what fails together and whether survivors can handle the peak.
exercise.solution: Check traffic failover/detection, data-layer availability and consistency, and survivor capacity. Also test shared authentication, DNS and configuration dependencies using the agreed user-visible indicator.

interview.question: What is the difference between availability and reliability?
interview.answer: Availability asks whether the required service is usable in its measurement window. Reliability is broader: consistent correct behavior across time and conditions. Define the actual user outcome before choosing a metric.
interview.followUp: Can a fast HTTP 200 response still represent a failed booking?

interview.question: Would you promise five nines for a small startup?
interview.answer: Only after requirements, architecture, operations and evidence support it. A stricter target increases redundancy and operating demands; start with a justified objective and measure an error budget.
interview.followUp: Which failure would you test first?

quiz.question: Two replicas share the only database. What remains?
options: A possible shared single point of failure
quiz.explanation: Application redundancy alone does not cover the shared database or its dependencies.

steps.title: Define success
steps.detail: For this example, success means a correct booking response within its latency objective. A homepage response alone does not measure the same user outcome.

steps.title: Spread the copies
steps.detail: Applications run in separate zones behind a resilient entry point. The goal is to avoid losing every application copy to the same local failure.

steps.title: Lose one zone
steps.detail: Zone A becomes unavailable. Detection and rerouting consume time, and requests already in flight may fail. The objective allows an explicitly measured error budget.

steps.title: Use remaining capacity
steps.detail: Zone B receives new work. It must have enough capacity, network access and working credentials to serve the actual user operation.

steps.title: Follow the data
steps.detail: Both application copies need a suitable data service. A single unprotected database can still interrupt bookings even when both application zones are healthy.

steps.title: Test the objective
steps.detail: Run a controlled failure and measure booking success and recovery time. Availability is demonstrated by user outcomes, not by counting boxes in a diagram.

title: Fault tolerance
simple: Fault tolerance is the ability to keep required behavior correct when specified components fail. Name the failure you tolerate and the degraded behavior you allow. It is not a claim of immunity to every possible fault.
analogy: A bicycle with a spare light can still be seen when the main light breaks. But that spare light cannot fix a broken frame. A useful plan names the fault and the remaining safe behavior. A website might keep showing events when its recommendation feature fails while refusing to sell a seat it cannot confirm.
why: A slow optional recommendation service should not use every request thread and prevent checkout. SeatSpot isolates optional work and keeps a safe core path instead of treating every dependency as equally critical.
engineering: Set timeouts based on a request deadline and propagate cancellation where supported. A dependency that never replies should not hold scarce resources forever. Bound concurrency separately for unrelated dependencies to limit the blast radius.

Retries can help transient failures but multiply load. Use a bounded attempt count, backoff and jitter, and only retry operations that are safe or protected by idempotency. A timeout does not prove the remote operation did nothing.

Choose degradation from business semantics. An older event description may be acceptable with a timestamp; inventing a payment result is not. Test partial failures and network timeouts, including a successful write whose response is lost.

worked.scenario: A page fans out to three optional services with an overall 800 ms deadline. One dependency stalls for ten seconds.
worked.calculation: A 200 ms dependency timeout can preserve some page budget, but sequential calls, retries and rendering time must also fit inside 800 ms. Timeouts are not independent free budgets.
worked.decision: Return the essential event page without recommendations; keep seat reservations and payment outcomes authoritative. Isolate resource pools so optional failures cannot consume core capacity.

implementation.explanation: This illustrates fallback for a genuinely optional read. Do not use an empty success result for a payment or booking operation. Runtime/schema validation and resource isolation are separate responsibilities.

useCases: Keeping optional features from taking down core operations.
Handling a specified node, network or dependency failure safely.
pitfalls: Retrying every error indefinitely.
Returning fabricated success after a payment timeout.
Testing only clean disconnections instead of partial failure.

exercise.prompt: The payment provider times out after you send a charge. What should the booking UI say and what should the backend do?
hints: A missing response does not prove a missing charge.
Use an operation identity that survives retries.
exercise.solution: Show a pending/unknown outcome rather than success or automatic failure. Reconcile by the same idempotency key/provider reference and update the order state. Avoid issuing a new independent charge.

interview.question: How do retries cause cascading failure?
interview.answer: They increase offered load while the dependency has reduced capacity. Bound attempts and concurrency, respect deadlines, add jitter and use a circuit breaker when appropriate.
interview.followUp: What changes when the operation is a non-idempotent write?

interview.question: Does graceful degradation always mean returning cached data?
interview.answer: No. The allowed fallback depends on correctness and privacy. Cached public descriptions may be acceptable; stale seat ownership or payment state may be unsafe.
interview.followUp: Which feature would you drop first in SeatSpot?

quiz.question: A timed-out charge means:
options: The provider definitely did not charge
The outcome may be unknown and needs reconciliation
The app should send ten new charges
quiz.explanation: Network failure can hide a successful remote write. Preserve operation identity and reconcile.

steps.title: Separate essential work
steps.detail: The event page needs correct booking information, but recommendations are optional. Give these paths different deadlines and resource budgets.

steps.title: An optional call stalls
steps.detail: Recommendations stop responding. Without a boundary, waiting calls can consume all connections or workers and affect otherwise healthy operations.

steps.title: Enforce a deadline
steps.detail: The timeout guard ends waiting for optional work. This protects local resources but does not prove a remote write was cancelled or never happened.

steps.title: Degrade honestly
steps.detail: Render the essential page without suggestions. Do not turn an uncertain payment outcome into a success message just to make the page appear healthy.

steps.title: Bound retries
steps.detail: If a retry is appropriate, limit attempts and use backoff with jitter. Preserve one operation identity for side effects so retries do not create duplicate business actions.

steps.title: Test partial failure
steps.detail: Inject a slow response and a lost reply in a safe test environment. Verify core capacity and user-visible correctness rather than only testing a clean server shutdown.

title: Horizontal scaling
simple: Horizontal scaling adds more machines or application copies. Work must be shareable between them. It differs from auto scaling: horizontal describes the direction of growth; automatic describes how the decision is made.
analogy: A teacher asks three helpers to check homework instead of giving one helper a faster pen. This helps if papers can be divided. It does not help much if every paper must wait for one locked answer book. Shared resources and coordination decide whether more helpers actually increase throughput.
why: SeatSpot can run several stateless event-page replicas during a sale. A user may reach a different copy on the next request, so login state, uploaded files and reservations cannot silently live only in one replica memory.
engineering: Separate process-local temporary state from durable shared state. Use a suitable session/token design and shared storage where necessary. Sticky sessions can reduce movement but do not preserve a lost server or make state replication automatic.

Parallel throughput is limited by serial work, locks, downstream quotas and coordination overhead. Measure the actual request mix. Scaling application reads does not automatically scale the primary database write path.

Plan node/zone distribution, load balancing and instance identity. Background jobs need safe work ownership; duplicate consumers must not perform the same side effect twice. More replicas also mean more connections and observability data.

worked.scenario: One replica safely serves 100 requests/second. A load test with four replicas reaches only 250.
worked.calculation: Ideal linear scaling would suggest 400, but the measured efficiency is 250/400 = 62.5%. This number describes the experiment, not a universal law.
worked.decision: Investigate database locking, shared CPU, connection limits and the serial part before adding another four replicas. Re-test after each change.

implementation.code:
# In a configured test Kubernetes cluster:
kubectl scale deployment/seatspot --replicas=4
kubectl get pods -l app=seatspot
# Verify readiness and run a controlled load test.
implementation.explanation: The scale command changes desired application replicas. It does not configure load balancing, storage, a cluster autoscaler or database capacity. An HPA may own this value in an automatically scaled deployment.

useCases: Stateless request processing and parallelizable jobs.
Distributing work and failure exposure across machines.
pitfalls: Assuming four replicas always give four times throughput.
Keeping sessions/files only on local ephemeral disk.
Ignoring extra downstream connections from each copy.

exercise.prompt: An upload is saved to App A local disk. The next download request reaches App B. Propose a fix.
hints: A load balancer does not copy files.
Distinguish durable object storage from a disposable application container.
exercise.solution: Store the file in a shared durable object store and keep metadata/access rules in an authoritative store. Stream or redirect authorized downloads from that shared location. Do not depend on sticky sessions for durability.

interview.question: What must change before scaling a stateful web process horizontally?
interview.answer: Identify session, file, cache and job state; choose ownership and persistence rules. Add routing/readiness and test a request moving between replicas.
interview.followUp: Which state should never be moved into a shared cache without a correctness decision?

interview.question: When will more replicas not help?
interview.answer: When serial work or a shared saturated dependency dominates. Measure tail latency, queueing and dependency waits before choosing the next scaling action.
interview.followUp: How would you prove that the database is limiting growth?

quiz.question: Horizontal scaling means:
quiz.explanation: Direction and automation are different decisions; adding copies can be manual.

steps.title: Start with one copy
steps.detail: One application serves event pages. Its safe measured capacity is finite, and a restart can interrupt every request reaching that copy.

steps.title: Add another copy
steps.detail: Deploy the same application on another machine or process. Horizontal scaling adds peers rather than increasing resources inside the original machine.

steps.title: Share incoming work
steps.detail: Routing sends requests to ready replicas. Balance according to workload characteristics; more boxes are useful only when requests can reach them.

steps.title: Move durable state
steps.detail: Both replicas use the same appropriate storage for files, sessions or records. A file written only to Replica A will not magically appear on Replica B.

steps.title: Find serial work
steps.detail: If every request waits on one locked database operation, extra applications may add waiting instead of throughput. Trace and load-test the complete path.

steps.title: Test the gain
steps.detail: Compare throughput and tail latency before and after scaling. Also remove one replica to check that remaining copies serve users correctly with available capacity.
steps.metric: Measure, do not assume linear gain

title: Vertical scaling
simple: Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, memory, storage or throughput. It can be the simplest improvement, but it has a size ceiling and does not create a second copy for failover.
analogy: A student replaces a tiny desk with a larger desk. More books fit, but there is still one desk. A bigger desk does not solve every problem: a lost key to the room still blocks access. Likewise, extra memory helps a memory bottleneck but may not help a slow external payment call.
why: A SeatSpot database may benefit from more memory for its working set before the team considers sharding. First measure the constraint rather than buying a larger machine because the site feels slow.
engineering: Inspect CPU, memory pressure, disk latency and database waits. More RAM may reduce reads from disk; more cores do not remove a serial lock or an external network delay.

An instance-size change can require a restart or failover, depending on the platform. Test supported upgrade paths, rollback and storage compatibility. Never promise downtime-free resizing without verifying the actual service.
Compare total cost and operational effort. Vertical scaling can buy time for a small team; it is not automatically a bad design. Maintain backups and redundancy independently.

worked.scenario: The database reads a 12 GB hot dataset but has only 4 GB available for useful caching.
worked.calculation: A larger memory budget may improve hit rate; the actual benefit depends on access patterns, other memory users and query plans. Doubling RAM is not a promise of double throughput.
worked.decision: Profile the working set and expensive queries, test a larger instance in a safe environment and measure tail latency and restart behavior.

implementation.code:
Measure -> resize in test -> repeat load test
Compare: p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory, I/O waits
Verify: restart/failover time and rollback plan
implementation.explanation: This is an operational experiment, not a browser-executable command or a recommendation for a particular paid machine.

useCases: Memory-bound databases or applications.
A measured short-term capacity increase with a manageable upgrade path.
pitfalls: Calling a larger machine highly available.
Resizing without checking restart behavior.
Ignoring an inefficient query that needs indexing.

exercise.prompt: CPU is idle but one SQL query waits on a lock. Will twice as many cores fix it?
hints: Identify the wait before choosing a resource.
Capacity and concurrency correctness are different.
exercise.solution: Probably not. Inspect the blocking transaction, query and locking strategy. Extra cores do not release the lock. Re-test after addressing the measured contention.

interview.question: Why choose vertical before horizontal scaling?
interview.answer: It can reduce coordination complexity when one larger instance meets requirements. Explain its limit, failure plan and tested upgrade path.
interview.followUp: What signals tell you that resizing has stopped helping?

interview.question: What remains after resizing?
interview.answer: Failure risk, backups, correctness and dependency bottlenecks remain. A bigger primary is still one primary.
interview.followUp: How would you roll back an unsuccessful upgrade?

quiz.question: A larger database server mainly guarantees:
options: More allocated resources on that server
quiz.explanation: Resource allocation and redundancy solve different problems.

steps.title: Measure the wait
steps.detail: The application is slow. Inspect whether requests wait on CPU, memory, storage, locks or another service before selecting a bigger machine.

steps.title: Increase resources
steps.detail: Give the same database more appropriate resources. This is vertical scaling because the number of independent database copies has not increased.

steps.title: Watch useful memory
steps.detail: More memory can hold more of the hot working set. If disk reads were the bottleneck, the experiment may show lower latency.

steps.title: Plan interruption
steps.detail: A size change may restart or fail over the database. Use the actual platform procedure and verify what users see during the transition.
steps.metric: Do not assume a live resize

steps.title: Retest the result
steps.detail: Repeat the same controlled workload. Compare throughput, tail latency, waits and cost; do not use machine size as the success metric.

steps.title: Keep a recovery plan
steps.detail: The larger machine still needs redundancy and backups. If the machine fails or reaches its size ceiling, a different design decision is needed.

title: Caching
simple: A cache keeps a reusable copy so future reads can avoid slower work. Copies can become stale or disappear. Decide what may be cached, for how long and who is allowed to read it.
analogy: You keep a timetable on your desk instead of walking to the office every time. It is fast, but a changed timetable makes your copy wrong. The expiry time tells you when to check again; it does not make the copy correct until then.
why: SeatSpot event descriptions change rarely and are read often. They are good cache candidates. Available-seat ownership and payment outcomes need stricter correctness rules than a public description.
engineering: In cache-aside, read the cache, fetch from the source on a miss, then populate the cache. The source remains authoritative. Define keys, TTL, invalidation and serialization; include tenant/user scope when needed.

A popular expired key can cause a cache stampede. Coalesce concurrent loads, add TTL jitter or use controlled stale-while-revalidate where staleness is allowed. Protect the source if the cache is unavailable.
Monitor hit rate, eviction and stale-result impact. A high hit rate can hide a very expensive miss path. Never cache private responses under a shared key that omits the authorization context.

worked.scenario: An illustrative endpoint receives 1,000 reads/second with an 80% cache hit rate.
worked.calculation: About 200 reads/second reach the source in the simplified model. After a cache outage, the source may suddenly receive all 1,000.
worked.decision: Test the cold-cache path, bound concurrent refill work and specify acceptable staleness for descriptions. Do not use the estimate to promise production capacity.

implementation.explanation: Illustrative pseudocode: cache/db adapters are not defined. Real code must handle errors, null values, concurrent misses, validation and invalidation.

useCases: Repeated expensive reads with an explicit staleness budget.
Public descriptions, computed summaries and suitable static assets.
pitfalls: Treating a cache as the only durable copy.
Caching private data with a public shared key.
Ignoring simultaneous misses after expiry.

exercise.prompt: An event title changes but users still see the old title. Explain two remedies.
hints: Identify the source of truth.
Expiry and invalidation have different timing.
exercise.solution: Invalidate or version the affected cache entry on a successful update, or accept the documented TTL staleness. Consider races between refill and update; test the chosen consistency behavior.

interview.question: How would you choose a TTL?
interview.answer: Start from the acceptable staleness, update rate, miss cost and refill load. Measure behavior rather than selecting a universal number.
interview.followUp: What happens when the hottest key expires?

interview.question: Should available seats be cached?
interview.answer: A read cache may support approximate browsing, but reservation correctness must be checked against authoritative state with concurrency control.
interview.followUp: How do you prevent two users booking the same seat?

quiz.question: When a cache disappears:
options: The source might receive a sudden load spike
All data must be permanently lost
quiz.explanation: A disposable cache needs a safe miss path and enough protection for its source.

steps.title: Request a description
steps.detail: The reader asks for a public event description. The key identifies the resource and representation; private results need appropriate identity scoping.

steps.title: Serve a hit
steps.detail: A reusable cached value returns quickly. Its age matters: a fast response can still be too stale for the business operation.

steps.title: Handle a miss
steps.detail: If the value is absent or expired, fetch from the source of truth. A miss is normal and must have bounded latency and safe error handling.

steps.title: Control refill work
steps.detail: Many readers may miss the same hot key together. Coalesce loads or bound refill work so the cache does not amplify pressure on the database.

steps.title: Store a temporary copy
steps.detail: Populate the cache with an explicit lifetime. Plan what happens after an update and whether serving an older value is acceptable during refresh.

steps.title: Test a cold cache
steps.detail: Remove the cache in a safe test. Observe source traffic, latency and errors. A warm hit-rate chart alone does not prove the architecture can recover.

title: CDN
simple: A content delivery network serves suitable content from locations closer to users. It can cache public assets and reduce origin traffic. It does not make private or rapidly changing data safe to cache automatically.
analogy: A publisher places copies of a book in many nearby libraries. A student borrows locally instead of travelling to the printing factory. A personalized sealed letter should not be put on the shared shelf. Similarly, images and versioned scripts differ from private booking responses.
why: SeatSpot posters and JavaScript bundles are useful near visitors. The booking API still needs authorization, correct seat state and an explicit cache policy.
engineering: Distinguish origin, edge cache and cache key. Query parameters, request headers and cookies can affect the representation. A key that combines different users can expose private content.
Use content-hashed names for immutable assets and appropriate Cache-Control. Replacing bytes behind the same long-cached name can leave older copies visible until expiry or invalidation.
CDN routing and cache state vary by location. Measure real-user latency and origin errors. A cache miss, dynamic route or invalidation still depends on the origin.

worked.scenario: An illustrative 1 MB poster is requested 10,000 times.
worked.calculation: Uncached origin transfer would be about 10 GB in decimal units. A 90% edge hit rate would reduce those origin payload reads to roughly 1 GB, ignoring overhead and refresh behavior.
worked.decision: Use explicit public asset policies and versioned filenames; treat booking/account routes separately. Costs, topology and actual hit rate depend on the provider and workload.

implementation.code:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
# Suitable only when the URL changes with the content:
/assets/event-poster.7f3a9c.webp

# Example private account response:
Cache-Control: private, no-store
implementation.explanation: Header examples, not a complete privacy policy. Verify behavior in browsers and intermediaries; do not apply an immutable public policy to personalized responses.

useCases: Global delivery of posters, stylesheets and versioned bundles.
Reducing repetitive public-content work at the origin.
pitfalls: Caching personalized responses without an identity-safe key.
Calling every CDN request a cache hit.
Replacing an immutable file without changing its URL.

exercise.prompt: A new logo is uploaded at the old immutable URL but users see the previous one. What is a safer release approach?
hints: Content identity belongs in the URL.
Updating source files is separate from deploying them.
exercise.solution: Deploy the new asset under a content-versioned URL and update references. Confirm the production deployment, response headers and edge behavior; invalidate legacy copies if necessary.

interview.question: Does a CDN remove the need for an origin?
interview.answer: No. Misses and noncached requests still need origin behavior unless content is fully hosted at the edge. Explain the request classes and failure paths.
interview.followUp: How would you test origin failure?

interview.question: How do you cache an authenticated API?
interview.answer: First decide whether caching is allowed. Private identity and authorization vary; bypassing shared cache may be safer. Explicitly validate cache keys and policies.
interview.followUp: Which cookie or header changes the response?

quiz.question: Which asset suits immutable public caching?
options: A changing account balance at one fixed URL
quiz.explanation: The URL changes with the bytes, so clients can retain that exact public representation.

steps.title: Choose the route
steps.detail: A visitor requests a public poster. The content delivery network routes the request to a suitable edge location rather than always going directly to the origin.

steps.title: Return a cached asset
steps.detail: If the edge has a valid copy, it returns that representation. This can reduce both response latency and repeated origin transfer.

steps.title: Fetch on a miss
steps.detail: A missing or expired representation needs an origin fetch. The origin and its network path still matter for uncached work.

steps.title: Use a versioned URL
steps.detail: When asset bytes change, publish a new content-versioned name. Long-lived immutable caching only fits a URL whose content will not change.

steps.title: Separate private data
steps.detail: An account or booking response may be personal and time-sensitive. Do not place it on the shared public cache path without a deliberately safe policy.

steps.title: Measure each path
steps.detail: Compare edge hits, misses and private requests separately. A fast cached poster does not show whether the booking API meets its latency and correctness objectives.

title: API gateway
simple: An API gateway is an entry layer that applies shared API policies and routes requests to services. Authentication, quotas and request validation may live there, but business authorization still belongs near the protected data.
analogy: A school reception desk checks visitor identity and sends visitors to the right office. Passing reception does not mean a visitor can open every cupboard. Services still decide which records or actions that person is permitted to access.
why: SeatSpot exposes event, order and payment services through one public API. Shared routing and coarse policies can be managed consistently, while each service owns its business rules.
engineering: An API gateway may terminate TLS, validate tokens, apply request limits and route by API version/path. A reverse proxy can overlap with these capabilities; these are roles, not necessarily separate products.

Verify token issuer, audience, expiry and signature using a maintained implementation. Do not trust user-supplied identity headers. The order service must still verify that this user owns the requested order.

Protect the gateway itself with capacity, redundancy and observability. Aggregating many downstream calls can create latency and failure coupling; define deadlines and keep the entry layer from becoming a large business-logic monolith.

worked.scenario: A mobile screen calls events and orders through one gateway.
worked.calculation: Its latency includes gateway work plus downstream waits. Two parallel calls take approximately the slower path plus overhead; two sequential calls add their delays. Real dependency behavior and timeouts determine the result.
worked.decision: Keep routing/coarse policy central but preserve domain authorization and tracing in services. Test a gateway outage and a single unhealthy downstream service.

implementation.code:
GET /api/events/:id  -> event service
GET /api/orders/:id  -> order service
Gateway: validate token, request size, coarse quota
Order service: verify ownership for this order
implementation.explanation: Architecture sketch only. Paths and policy wording are illustrative, not a deployed gateway or complete authentication implementation.

useCases: A managed public boundary for several APIs.
Consistent token validation, coarse quotas and version routing.
pitfalls: Assuming token validation proves ownership of every resource.
Forwarding client-supplied identity headers as trusted identity.
Creating one unbounded aggregation request.

exercise.prompt: A signed-in user changes an order ID in the URL. Which component must stop cross-user access?
hints: Authentication answers who, not whether this order belongs to them.
Enforce ownership in the data/service boundary.
exercise.solution: The order service must perform resource-level authorization using verified identity. Gateway checks are useful but cannot replace ownership enforcement.

interview.question: API gateway versus reverse proxy?
interview.answer: A reverse proxy forwards requests on behalf of servers. An API gateway specializes that entry role with API-facing policy and lifecycle features; one product may perform both.
interview.followUp: What logic should stay out of the gateway?

interview.question: What is your gateway failure strategy?
interview.answer: Use a suitably redundant entry tier, bounded work and observability. Analyze whether bypass is safe; bypassing authentication or limits is not an acceptable automatic fallback.
interview.followUp: How do you rotate validation keys safely?

quiz.question: A valid access token means:
options: The user may read every order
Identity may be established, but resource authorization is still needed
quiz.explanation: Authentication and resource-level authorization solve different questions.

steps.title: Enter one API boundary
steps.detail: The client calls a public API address. The gateway provides a shared routing boundary instead of requiring clients to know every internal service location.

steps.title: Apply coarse policy
steps.detail: Validate the request and supported identity credentials with maintained security libraries. Reject oversized or invalid traffic before forwarding expensive work.

steps.title: Route by responsibility
steps.detail: Event requests go to the event service; order requests go to the order service. API versions and paths should have deliberate routing rules.

steps.title: Authorize the record
steps.detail: The order service checks ownership and allowed actions using verified identity. Passing gateway authentication does not grant access to another visitor order.

steps.title: Bound aggregation
steps.detail: If one API request fans out, set deadlines and partial-failure behavior. A slow optional service should not hold every gateway worker indefinitely.

steps.title: Operate the entry tier
steps.detail: Trace requests through the boundary and test gateway capacity and redundancy. Centralizing policy is useful, but it also creates an important operational dependency.

title: Rate limiting
simple: Rate limiting controls how much work an identity or client may request over time. It protects capacity and fairness, but it is not a complete defense against every attack.
analogy: A library lets each student borrow a limited number of books so one student cannot empty the shelves. A short burst may be acceptable, but repeated borrowing must remain within a fair rate. The rule needs a reliable way to identify the student, not just the colour of their shoes.
why: SeatSpot protects sign-in and booking attempts from excessive traffic. Public browsing, expensive searches and paid customers may need different budgets; one shared limit for everyone can punish unrelated users.
engineering: Define the principal, scope, sustained rate and burst capacity. A token bucket refills tokens over time; requests consume them. A fixed window is simpler but can admit a boundary burst across adjacent windows.

In a distributed service, per-process counters are not a strict global limit. Use appropriate atomic shared state or a deliberately partitioned budget. Document any best-effort behavior and what happens when the limiter store is unavailable.

A 429 response should communicate a safe retry policy where appropriate. Combine limits with bounded concurrency, authentication and abuse controls. Do not trust a spoofable forwarded-IP header or identify all users behind one NAT as one person without considering fairness.

worked.scenario: A teaching token bucket has capacity 10 and refills at 2 tokens/second.
worked.calculation: If initially full, ten immediate requests can consume ten tokens. After 3 idle seconds it has six tokens, capped at ten. This model ignores distributed races until an atomic implementation is chosen.
worked.decision: Choose a key and storage behavior explicitly. Protect critical actions with a deliberate fail-closed or degraded policy rather than silently giving unlimited access after a store failure.

implementation.explanation: Conceptual single-key token-bucket algorithm. Reading, refilling and consuming must be atomic for a shared distributed limiter. It is not production middleware.

useCases: Protecting costly or abuse-prone API actions.
Per-tenant fairness and upstream quota protection.
pitfalls: Using independent instance counters as a global guarantee.
Trusting client-provided IP identity.
Retrying 429 responses immediately in a tight loop.

exercise.prompt: Three replicas each allow 100 requests/minute for one user. Is the global user limit 100?
hints: Ask where the state lives.
A client can reach different replicas.
exercise.solution: Not with independent counters: the user may receive up to roughly 300 across replicas, depending on routing and windows. Use an atomic shared budget or state explicitly that the policy is per instance.

interview.question: Token bucket or fixed window?
interview.answer: Explain sustained rate, burst tolerance, boundary behavior and storage cost. Pick the policy from requirements and test concurrent enforcement.
interview.followUp: What state must be updated atomically?

interview.question: What if Redis is down?
interview.answer: Choose fail-closed, fallback or limited degraded behavior per endpoint risk. Alert and bound capacity; do not silently pretend a global guarantee still holds.
interview.followUp: Would browsing and payment creation use the same fallback?

quiz.question: Why can a fixed window admit a large short burst?
options: Requests near the end and start of adjacent windows use different budgets
quiz.explanation: Window boundaries can allow two budgets in a short interval. Choose the intended burst semantics.

steps.title: Identify the principal
steps.detail: Requests are assigned a deliberate identity key, such as a verified account and endpoint. A spoofable header cannot safely define a protected client budget.

steps.title: Refill the budget
steps.detail: The token bucket refills over elapsed time up to its capacity. Capacity permits a bounded burst while the refill rate controls sustained use.

steps.title: Consume atomically
steps.detail: Checking and consuming a token must behave as one operation for shared state. Separate reads and writes can overspend under concurrency.

steps.title: Allow affordable work
steps.detail: A request with enough tokens proceeds, but still faces authorization, request validation and downstream concurrency limits. Passing the limiter is not a correctness guarantee.

steps.title: Reject excess traffic
steps.detail: A request without budget receives a clear rejection and retry guidance where appropriate. Clients should wait rather than creating an immediate retry storm.

steps.title: Plan storage failure
steps.detail: If the shared limiter fails, enforce the chosen endpoint policy and alert. Independent local counters do not preserve a strict global quota across replicas.

title: Circuit breaker
simple: A circuit breaker temporarily stops calls to a dependency that appears unhealthy, then cautiously tests recovery. It prevents repeated waiting and extra pressure; it does not repair the dependency.
analogy: A home fuse interrupts an unsafe circuit instead of letting every appliance keep drawing current. A software breaker is not the same physical mechanism, but the useful idea is similar: stop repeated harmful attempts, observe conditions and restore access carefully.
why: If SeatSpot recommendations repeatedly time out, continuing to call them can occupy every connection. A breaker can reject or use a safe optional fallback while core booking work continues.
engineering: Closed means normal calls are allowed while failures are measured. Open means calls are rejected quickly for a period. Half-open allows a limited probe set; success can close the breaker and failure can reopen it.

Define eligible failures, a minimum sample, threshold, window and reset policy. A small number of failures at low traffic can mislead a naive ratio. Per-instance breakers can reach different states, which must be understood operationally.

Combine timeouts, concurrency isolation and bounded retries. A breaker protects resources only if requests cannot pile up elsewhere. Fallback must preserve business meaning; do not fabricate a successful charge.

worked.scenario: An illustrative breaker opens after enough samples show a 50% eligible-failure rate in its window.
worked.calculation: A minimum of 20 calls avoids opening after one failure out of one call in this example. The numbers are teaching choices, not recommended universal settings.
worked.decision: Define which timeouts/errors count, limit half-open probes and watch false trips alongside recovery time.

implementation.code:
CLOSED: allow calls and record eligible outcomes
OPEN: reject quickly or use a safe fallback
After reset interval -> HALF_OPEN
HALF_OPEN: limited probes; success -> CLOSED
Failed probe -> OPEN
implementation.explanation: State-machine sketch only. Production libraries must handle concurrency, cancellation and metric windows correctly.

useCases: Isolating an unhealthy dependency.
Fast optional fallback during repeated remote failures.
pitfalls: Treating an open breaker as proof of root cause.
Allowing every caller to probe recovery at once.
Returning fake success for essential writes.

exercise.prompt: What should a breaker do after the reset interval?
hints: Allow a small probe set.
Avoid sending all queued work immediately.
exercise.solution: Move to half-open with bounded probes. Evaluate actual outcomes before restoring full traffic; otherwise recovering capacity may be overwhelmed again.

interview.question: Circuit breaker versus retry?
interview.answer: Retry attempts an operation again; a breaker stops attempts temporarily when failure evidence justifies it. They need a shared time and load budget.
interview.followUp: Can retries stop the breaker from detecting real errors?

interview.question: How do you select a threshold?
interview.answer: Use traffic volume, failure types, latency objective and cost of false trips. Include minimum samples and test recovery rather than copying arbitrary percentages.
interview.followUp: How does low request volume change the design?

quiz.question: Half-open should usually:
options: Let every caller through at once
quiz.explanation: Limited probes avoid overwhelming a dependency before recovery is established.

steps.title: Closed: calls flow
steps.detail: The breaker allows normal calls and records eligible outcomes. Timeouts still bound each attempt; a closed breaker is not a guarantee of health.

steps.title: Observe repeated failures
steps.detail: The dependency times out repeatedly. A minimum sample and measurement window help distinguish a pattern from a single unlucky request.

steps.title: Open: stop pressure
steps.detail: The breaker opens and rejects dependency calls quickly. This frees local resources and avoids repeating expensive failures while recovery is investigated.

steps.title: Choose an honest fallback
steps.detail: Optional recommendations can be omitted. Essential payment outcomes must remain pending or failed according to verified state, not invented to hide the outage.

steps.title: Half-open: probe
steps.detail: After a reset interval, allow a limited probe set. Sending every waiting caller at once can overload a dependency that is only partly recovered.

steps.title: Recover or reopen
steps.detail: Successful probes restore normal traffic; failed probes reopen the breaker. Observe both false trips and recovery behavior under controlled failure tests.

title: Message queues
simple: A message queue holds work until a consumer can process it. It separates accepting work from finishing it. Durability, retries, ordering and duplicate delivery depend on the queue and configuration.
analogy: A restaurant writes orders on tickets. The cook takes a ticket when ready instead of making every customer stand at the stove. A ticket can be picked up twice after confusion, so the kitchen needs an order number to avoid preparing and charging the same order twice.
why: SeatSpot sends receipts asynchronously after booking. The booking request should not wait for an email provider, but it must reliably record that a receipt needs to be sent.
engineering: Producers publish jobs; consumers receive, process and acknowledge them. A crash before acknowledgment can cause redelivery. Design idempotent business effects using a stable job ID and durable deduplication where required.

Backlog is stored delay, not free capacity. Monitor oldest-message age, arrival rate, service rate, retention and dead-letter messages. If arrivals exceed safe processing over time, the queue grows until a limit is reached.

To coordinate a database commit and publication, consider a transactional outbox: commit business state and an outgoing record together, then relay it with duplicate-safe consumers. A database transaction cannot automatically include an unrelated broker.

worked.scenario: Jobs arrive at 90/second and each worker safely processes 20/second.
worked.calculation: Four workers provide 80/second, so backlog grows by about 10/second. Five provide 100/second and drain only about 10/second of existing backlog in the simplified model.
worked.decision: Add safe capacity or shed work, respecting the email provider quota. More consumers are not safe if they collectively exceed the next dependency limit.

implementation.code:
BEGIN
  insert booking
  insert outbox(event_id, type="ReceiptRequested", booking_id)
COMMIT
Relay: publish outbox event; retry safely
Consumer: apply effect once per event_id; acknowledge
implementation.explanation: Conceptual outbox flow. A real implementation needs polling/CDC, durable state, concurrent ownership and an external side-effect reconciliation strategy.

useCases: Background receipts, exports and image processing.
Smoothing bursts within measured processing capacity.
pitfalls: Acknowledging before durable work is safe.
Assuming at-least-once delivery prevents duplicates.
Treating the queue as an unlimited buffer.

exercise.prompt: A worker sends an email then crashes before acknowledging. What happens?
hints: The job may be delivered again.
The effect and the acknowledgment are different events.
exercise.solution: Redelivery may send another email unless the consumer/provider has an idempotency or deduplication strategy. A durable order/event identity and reconciliation make this case explicit.

interview.question: How do you handle poison messages?
interview.answer: Bound attempts, move persistent failures to a dead-letter path, alert and provide a controlled repair/replay process. Do not silently discard business-critical work.
interview.followUp: What if the replay schema has changed?

interview.question: Does a queue give exactly-once effects?
interview.answer: Not universally. Broker delivery guarantees and external business effects differ. Explain acknowledgment gaps, idempotency and the scope of any deduplication guarantee.
interview.followUp: How do you make an external payment safe?

quiz.question: A crash before acknowledgment may cause:
options: Automatic rollback of an email already sent
quiz.explanation: The queue can retry delivery but cannot unsend an external side effect.

steps.title: Record outgoing work
steps.detail: A booking succeeds and records a receipt job reliably. Coordinate this with business storage, for example using an outbox, so a crash does not lose the obligation.

steps.title: Buffer a burst
steps.detail: The queue stores work while consumers catch up. Stored backlog buys time, but retention, storage and acceptable delay remain finite.

steps.title: Process within limits
steps.detail: Workers pull jobs at a safe rate. Their combined concurrency must respect email provider quotas and other downstream capacity.

steps.title: A worker crashes
steps.detail: A worker can send an email and fail before acknowledging its job. The queue may deliver that same logical job again.

steps.title: Protect the effect
steps.detail: Use stable job identity and an appropriate idempotency or reconciliation strategy. A delivery guarantee alone does not guarantee exactly one external effect.

steps.title: Handle persistent failure
steps.detail: After bounded attempts, move a poison job to a monitored dead-letter path. Investigate and repair before controlled replay instead of retrying forever.

title: Event-driven architecture
simple: In event-driven architecture, components announce facts that happened and other components react. An event such as BookingConfirmed differs from a command such as ConfirmBooking, which asks an owner to perform an action.
analogy: A school posts that sports day has been confirmed. Teachers arrange transport, the canteen plans food and students bring equipment. The announcement is one fact with several independent reactions. If the date is corrected, people need a clear update rather than silently rewriting an announcement they already acted on.
why: SeatSpot booking confirmation can trigger receipts, analytics and loyalty updates without the booking service synchronously calling every consumer. This reduces direct coupling but introduces asynchronous coordination.
engineering: Publish event identity, type, version, time and the minimum useful payload. Choose commands versus facts deliberately. Avoid unnecessary personal data because events can be retained or copied to many consumers.

Assume duplicates, late arrivals and ordering limits unless the actual system guarantees otherwise. Consumers must be idempotent, handle compatible schema evolution and monitor their own lag and failure paths.

Independent reactions do not create one cross-service atomic transaction. Use a workflow/saga and compensating actions when needed, with a clear owner and recoverable state. An event log is not automatically a complete event-sourced model.

worked.scenario: BookingConfirmed has receipt, analytics and loyalty subscribers.
worked.calculation: A failed analytics consumer should not roll back a valid booking. Loyalty may remain eventually consistent, while seat ownership must stay authoritative.
worked.decision: Document each subscriber obligation and recovery/replay rules. Replaying an analytics event is different from sending every historical receipt again.

implementation.code:
{
  "id": "evt-42",
  "type": "BookingConfirmed",
  "version": 1,
  "bookingId": "bk-17",
  "occurredAt": "2026-11-20T10:00:00Z"
}
implementation.explanation: Fictional event contract. Use real unique IDs, schema checks, access control and a deliberately chosen publication/durability strategy.

useCases: Independent reactions to business facts.
Integration where temporary consumer delay is acceptable.
pitfalls: Calling every message an event.
Assuming global ordering across all consumers.
Replaying side effects without a replay policy.

exercise.prompt: A loyalty consumer receives BookingConfirmed twice. What must remain true?
hints: The event ID is stable across redelivery.
Awarding points is a business effect.
exercise.solution: The booking should earn the intended points once. Deduplicate or make the update idempotent within a durable transaction; account for partial failure around external effects.

interview.question: What do you gain and lose with events?
interview.answer: Gain looser direct coupling and independent consumption. Accept eventual consistency, operational lag, schema management and harder end-to-end debugging.
interview.followUp: When would a synchronous call be simpler?

interview.question: How do you evolve an event?
interview.answer: Prefer compatible additive changes, version deliberately, validate consumers and plan retention/replay. Avoid changing the meaning of an existing field silently.
interview.followUp: How does a slow old consumer survive deployment?

quiz.question: Which is a fact rather than a command?
quiz.explanation: An event describes something that already happened; a command requests work.

steps.title: Commit a business fact
steps.detail: The booking owner establishes that the booking is confirmed, then reliably publishes the associated fact. Publication and storage must have an explicit failure strategy.

steps.title: Fan out independently
steps.detail: The event channel makes the fact available to separate subscribers. Each subscriber has a distinct business responsibility and its own processing state.

steps.title: One subscriber lags
steps.detail: Analytics becomes slow while receipt processing continues. Subscriber delay is observable; it should not silently redefine the original booking outcome.

steps.title: Deliver the event twice
steps.detail: A repeated delivery uses the same logical event identity. Consumers must avoid awarding points or producing another external effect accidentally.

steps.title: Evolve the contract
steps.detail: Add compatible fields carefully and test old consumers. Retained events and delayed subscribers may outlive the latest deployment.

steps.title: Plan recovery and replay
steps.detail: Replay analytics when appropriate, but do not resend historical receipts automatically. Reprocessing policy depends on the side effects owned by each subscriber.

title: Database replication
simple: Replication keeps copies of database data. It can improve resilience or serve reads, but asynchronous copies may lag. A replica is not the same as an independent backup.
analogy: Two students copy notes from one teacher. If copying takes time, one notebook may lack the last sentence. If the teacher accidentally deletes an important page and the students copy that deletion, every notebook can lose it. You still need a recoverable older copy.
why: SeatSpot may serve public catalog reads from replicas while routing authoritative reservations to the write owner. A user reading immediately after a write must not be surprised by a stale confirmation state.
engineering: In primary/replica arrangements, writes are accepted by the primary and changes are shipped to replicas. Asynchronous acknowledgment can be faster but may leave an acknowledged write unavailable after a primary loss before replication.

Synchronous replication can wait for specified remote durability/visibility guarantees, adding latency or reducing write availability when required replicas cannot reply. Inspect the database-specific guarantee rather than using the word synchronous loosely.

Failover needs promotion rules, client reconnection and fencing of the old writer. Two independent primaries can diverge. Monitor replication lag and use a read-your-writes strategy, such as routing a user to the primary temporarily, when necessary.

worked.scenario: The primary confirms a booking at 12:00:00. A read replica applies it at 12:00:02.
worked.calculation: A read at 12:00:01 may see the earlier state. Two seconds here is fictional teaching lag, not a product guarantee.
worked.decision: Read the confirmation from an authoritative path or implement a documented consistency mechanism. Do not tell the user their purchase disappeared simply because a replica is behind.

implementation.explanation: Read-only diagnostic examples, not a complete replication setup. Permissions, monitoring access and column details depend on the actual database version/service.

useCases: Read distribution where staleness is acceptable.
Maintaining copies for defined failover scenarios.
pitfalls: Using replication instead of backups.
Promoting a new writer without fencing the old one.
Ignoring read-after-write behavior.

exercise.prompt: Why can a replica show an order as missing just after checkout?
hints: Follow when the write was acknowledged and applied.
Not every read path has the same consistency.
exercise.solution: Asynchronous replication may not have applied the write yet. Route that confirmation to an appropriate authoritative path or use a supported read-your-writes mechanism. Distinguish lag from a real failed write.

interview.question: Synchronous or asynchronous replication?
interview.answer: Choose from durability, latency and availability requirements. State exactly what an acknowledgment means and what can be lost during failover.
interview.followUp: What happens if the required synchronous replica is unreachable?

interview.question: Why retain backups?
interview.answer: Replication can copy accidental deletes or corruption. Backups and point-in-time recovery address different recovery needs and must be restore-tested.
interview.followUp: How do you validate a restored backup?

quiz.question: Which statement is safest?
options: A replica may lag and is not a backup replacement
quiz.explanation: Consistency and recovery guarantees depend on replication and failover configuration.

steps.title: Write at the owner
steps.detail: A booking write reaches the current primary. Its acknowledgment policy determines what the application can assume about durability and replication at that moment.

steps.title: Ship changes
steps.detail: Changes travel to replicas. With asynchronous replication, the primary can reply before all copies have applied the latest write.

steps.title: Read a lagging copy
steps.detail: A confirmation read reaches Replica A before the booking arrives there. The user may see an older state even though the primary accepted the write.

steps.title: Choose a consistent path
steps.detail: Use the primary or an explicitly supported consistency mechanism for confirmation. Public catalog reads can have a different staleness allowance.

steps.title: Coordinate failover
steps.detail: If the primary fails, promotion needs a clear election or orchestration process and fencing. Avoid letting an isolated old writer accept conflicting new changes.

steps.title: Keep recovery separate
steps.detail: Replication also copies many mistakes. Maintain tested backups and recovery points independently rather than counting live copies as protection against every kind of data loss.

title: Database sharding
simple: Sharding divides records across separate database shards, often using a key. Each record needs a known home. It can spread storage and write load, but cross-shard operations and moving data become harder.
analogy: A library splits books across buildings by a catalog rule. The catalog must tell you which building owns a book. A rule that sends every popular book to the same building still creates a queue. Finding books across all buildings is more work than visiting one shelf.
why: SeatSpot may eventually outgrow one database write/storage boundary. Sharding could place different tenants or events on different shards, but one extremely popular event can still create a hot shard.
engineering: Choose the shard key from access patterns, distribution, locality and growth. Hashing spreads keys but does not guarantee evenly distributed workload. Range sharding helps ordered access but may concentrate newest or popular data.

Keep a routing map/version and plan online rebalancing, ownership transfer and rollback. A simple modulo change remaps many keys; consistent hashing reduces some movement but does not eliminate migration and hot-key problems.

Cross-shard joins, transactions, uniqueness and global ordering need explicit support or application redesign. Try indexing, query fixes, vertical growth or read distribution first when they meet the actual requirement more simply.

worked.scenario: Ten tenants each produce similar load except one tenant generates half the total.
worked.calculation: Hashing tenant IDs across four shards can still put half the traffic on the hot tenant shard. Even key counts do not mean even traffic.
worked.decision: Consider splitting that tenant workload using a suitable finer key, isolation or an alternative ownership model. Test query patterns and transaction boundaries before committing.

implementation.explanation: Do not increase 4 to 5 in a live system and assume existing rows move automatically. Routing and stored ownership must change through a controlled migration.

useCases: Write/storage growth beyond a suitable single database boundary.
Tenant isolation with carefully chosen access patterns.
pitfalls: Confusing many logical table partitions with separate physical shards.
Ignoring cross-shard transactions and global uniqueness.
Treating hash distribution as a guarantee against hot keys.

exercise.prompt: One event causes 70% of booking writes and eventId is the shard key. Does adding shards fix it?
hints: The hot event stays one key.
More shards help only if its work can be partitioned safely.
exercise.solution: Not automatically. That event remains on one shard. Revisit seat ownership/partitioning and concurrency rules, or provide dedicated capacity, without weakening atomic reservation correctness.

interview.question: How do you choose a shard key?
interview.answer: Use dominant reads/writes, locality, growth and skew; test hot entities and cross-shard operations. Explain migration and ownership, not just a hash function.
interview.followUp: How would a single large tenant change your choice?

interview.question: What makes resharding difficult?
interview.answer: Routing and data location must stay consistent during copy and cutover. Handle writes, retries, verification and rollback while preventing conflicting ownership.
interview.followUp: Can both old and new shards accept writes during migration?

quiz.question: A shard key with evenly many rows guarantees:
options: Neither even load nor safe cross-shard transactions
quiz.explanation: Data volume, request frequency and coordination are distinct concerns.

steps.title: Identify the record home
steps.detail: A request carries a tenant or entity key. The routing rule maps that key to an authoritative shard before data is read or written.

steps.title: Distribute independent records
steps.detail: Different record groups live on different database shards. This can spread storage and write work when the groups are actually independent enough.

steps.title: Find a hot key
steps.detail: One popular event can overload its shard even when every shard has the same row count. Workload distribution matters more than counting keys.

steps.title: Examine a global query
steps.detail: A query across all events may contact every shard and merge results. Cross-shard joins, transactions and uniqueness require deliberate support or redesign.

steps.title: Move ownership safely
steps.detail: Rebalancing needs copying, verification, a write/cutover policy and an updated routing map. Changing a modulo number does not move existing records.

steps.title: Choose the simplest fit
steps.detail: Shard only when requirements and measurements justify the coordination cost. A suitable index or larger database may solve the current problem with much less complexity.

title: Data partitioning
simple: Partitioning splits a dataset into manageable parts using rules such as date ranges or key hashes. Table partitions can remain inside one database; partitioning does not automatically mean physical sharding across servers.
analogy: You organize school papers into folders by month. Finding November work becomes easier if you open only the November folder. Putting every folder on the same desk does not create more desks. Likewise, smaller table parts can improve maintenance or pruning without adding another database machine.
why: SeatSpot stores an increasing audit/history table. Date partitions can make retention and time-bounded queries easier while keeping current reservation transactions on an appropriate authoritative path.
engineering: Match the partition key to queries and lifecycle operations. Partition pruning avoids irrelevant parts when predicates and the database plan permit it. A query with no usable partition condition may still scan many partitions.

Range, list and hash partitions have different properties. Plan creation of future partitions, default/error behavior for unmatched rows, indexes and retention. Too many tiny partitions can add planning and management overhead.

Check uniqueness and foreign-key capabilities in the specific database. Partitioning may constrain global uniqueness or maintenance operations. It does not remove the need for indexing or automatically solve write contention on one hot record.

worked.scenario: History contains one million rows per month over two years. A query requests one month.
worked.calculation: With useful pruning it may inspect a relevant partition rather than all 24 million rows, but actual I/O depends on predicates, indexes and plans.
worked.decision: Use EXPLAIN in a test environment. Confirm pruning and retention behavior instead of assuming a partitioned table is always faster.

implementation.explanation: PostgreSQL teaching example. The lower bound is inclusive and upper bound exclusive. Insertions outside defined partitions need another matching/default partition; indexes and constraints are not complete here.

useCases: Time-based history retention and maintenance.
Queries that can select a limited set of data partitions.
pitfalls: Calling all partitioning sharding.
Missing future partition creation.
Ignoring query plans and global constraint behavior.

exercise.prompt: A table is partitioned by date, but a query filters only customer email. Must it be fast?
hints: Ask whether the date partitions can be pruned.
A suitable index can still matter.
exercise.solution: No. The engine may inspect many partitions without a useful date restriction. Examine the actual plan and indexing/access pattern rather than assuming partitioning alone helps.

interview.question: Partitioning versus sharding?
interview.answer: Partitioning is splitting data by a rule. Sharding usually distributes those groups across separate data owners/servers. State the physical topology and transaction boundary.
interview.followUp: Can a partitioned table still be one failure domain?

interview.question: How would you expire old history?
interview.answer: Use a retention policy, verify dependencies/backup requirements, then perform the database-supported partition lifecycle operation safely. Dropping data is not a reversible performance trick.
interview.followUp: What must happen before removing the oldest partition?

quiz.question: Date partitioning helps most when:
options: Queries can eliminate irrelevant date partitions
All rows share one locked counter
quiz.explanation: Useful pruning depends on predicates and the chosen partition design.

steps.title: Define a partition rule
steps.detail: History rows are grouped by date. This organization can exist inside one database and should not be confused with distributing ownership across independent shards.

steps.title: Create ranges
steps.detail: Each month has a defined range with explicit boundaries. Future data needs a matching partition or a deliberately configured default behavior.

steps.title: Ask for November
steps.detail: A date-bounded query reaches the planner. The engine can eliminate irrelevant ranges if its rules and the query expression permit partition pruning.

steps.title: Read the useful part
steps.detail: The November partition supplies the requested history. An appropriate index and query plan can still be necessary inside that partition.

steps.title: Maintain the lifecycle
steps.detail: Retention can operate on old partitions, but removal is a data-policy decision. Verify dependencies, recovery requirements and correct boundaries before destructive maintenance.

steps.title: Know the boundary
steps.detail: A query without the partition key may still inspect many parts. More partitions do not automatically add machines, guarantee speed or fix one hot-row lock.

title: Microservices
simple: Microservices split a system into independently deployable business services. The useful boundary is ownership of a capability and its data, not an arbitrary number of small functions or servers.
analogy: A school has a library team, accounts team and transport team. Each owns a different responsibility and communicates through clear requests. If every tiny task needs a meeting with every team, work becomes slower. More teams are helpful only when their boundaries reduce coordination rather than create it.
