why: SeatSpot may separate booking, catalog and notifications when team ownership, scaling or deployment needs justify it. A small team can often start with a modular monolith and preserve those boundaries without network overhead.
engineering: Choose boundaries from domain invariants and team ownership. Avoid a shared database schema that every service edits freely; it couples deployments even if applications have different names.

Network calls fail partially and add latency. Cross-service updates need explicit workflows, idempotency and reconciliation. A local transaction cannot automatically protect a business invariant spread across unrelated stores.

Independent deployment requires compatible contracts, observability, testing and operations. If services must always deploy together, investigate whether the boundary or shared dependencies are wrong.

worked.scenario: A confirmation requires catalog lookup, seat reservation, payment and notification.
worked.calculation: Putting all four behind sequential network calls increases latency and failure combinations. Notification can be asynchronous; reservation/payment need an explicit state machine and reconciliation.
worked.decision: Start with the required invariant and workflow. Separate a capability only when the autonomy benefit outweighs the distributed coordination cost.

implementation.code:
Catalog: owns public event descriptions
Booking: owns seat reservation state
Payments: owns provider integration and reconciliation
Notifications: owns delivery jobs
Contracts connect owners; services do not edit each other tables.
implementation.explanation: A proposed domain sketch, not a claim that all systems need four services or that network calls provide atomic transactions.

useCases: Independent teams or capabilities with different release/scaling needs.
Domains with clear data and operation ownership.
pitfalls: Splitting by technical layer into chatty services.
Sharing mutable tables without ownership.
Treating a modular monolith as inherently inferior.

exercise.prompt: A two-person team has low traffic and no independent deployment needs. Must it use microservices?
hints: Compare operational cost with the actual requirement.
Preserve boundaries without requiring network calls.
exercise.solution: No. A modular monolith can keep clear domains with simpler transactions and operations. Revisit extraction when measured scaling, ownership or release constraints justify it.

interview.question: How would you choose service boundaries?
interview.answer: Find business capabilities, invariants, data ownership and team responsibilities. Model the workflow and failure paths before deciding which boundary becomes a network call.
interview.followUp: Which invariant should remain inside one owner?

interview.question: What is a distributed monolith?
interview.answer: Services are physically separate but tightly coupled through shared tables, synchronous dependencies or coordinated releases. The operational cost exists without much autonomy.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce one such coupling?

quiz.question: A strong reason to split a service is:
options: Every class needs its own server
A clear independent capability and justified ownership/deployment need
quiz.explanation: Autonomy must justify the added network and operational complexity.

steps.title: Find the capabilities
steps.detail: Name business responsibilities before drawing services. Catalog descriptions and authoritative seat reservations have different ownership and correctness requirements.

steps.title: Own the data
steps.detail: Each capability owns its protected state and exposes contracts. Giving every service write access to every table defeats much of the intended independence.

steps.title: Cross a network boundary
steps.detail: The booking workflow contacts payments. That call can time out or succeed remotely while its response is lost; it is not a local transaction.

steps.title: Decouple optional work
steps.detail: Confirmation can publish notification work after reliable business-state coordination. A slow email provider need not occupy the booking request indefinitely.

steps.title: Deploy compatibly
steps.detail: Old and new callers may coexist. Test contract compatibility and observe version-specific errors instead of requiring every service to deploy in lockstep.

steps.title: Justify the complexity
steps.detail: For a small team, a modular monolith may satisfy the same domain boundaries with fewer moving parts. Choose services from requirements rather than fashion.

title: Service discovery
simple: Service discovery maps a stable service name to current usable destinations. Instances change as they deploy, fail or scale. Discovery finds candidates; routing and health policies decide how requests reach them.
analogy: A school directory lists which rooms currently host each club. Students ask for the chess club rather than memorizing an old room number. The directory can become stale, so someone must update it and decide what happens when a listed room is closed.
why: SeatSpot booking replicas should find the payment service even when its pod addresses change. Hard-coded ephemeral IPs become stale during routine operations.
engineering: Discovery can be DNS-based, registry-based or platform-provided. Client-side discovery chooses an instance in the caller; server-side discovery can expose a stable proxy/service address. Clarify which layer owns selection.

Registration, readiness, deregistration and stale caches affect routing. Name resolution can succeed while a returned endpoint is unusable. DNS TTL and connection reuse influence how quickly callers observe changes.
Secure the registry and service identity. Discoverability is not authorization. Timeouts, bounded retries and observability remain necessary when a resolved instance fails.

worked.scenario: Three payment pods are replaced during a rolling deployment.
worked.calculation: Their individual IPs may change while a Kubernetes Service name remains stable. Endpoint/readiness propagation and existing connections still create a transition interval.
worked.decision: Use the platform service abstraction and test replacement with live requests. Do not promise instantaneous convergence from a stable name.

implementation.code:
http://payments.default.svc.cluster.local:8080
# Example Kubernetes Service DNS name inside a configured cluster.
# Deployment/pod addresses may change behind the service.
implementation.explanation: This is a private cluster naming example, not an internet URL or a working endpoint supplied by Sukoaa. Service definition, namespace and network policy must exist.

useCases: Dynamic replica sets and container platforms.
Locating current service endpoints without hard-coded pod IPs.
pitfalls: Treating discovery as authentication.
Caching endpoint addresses forever.
Ignoring readiness and stale connections.

exercise.prompt: DNS resolves the service but requests fail. What do you check next?
hints: A name is only one part of the path.
Inspect endpoints, readiness, ports and policy.
exercise.solution: Check ready endpoints, target port, network reachability/policy, TLS identity and the dependency itself. Compare resolution with an actual bounded request and inspect traces.

interview.question: Discovery versus load balancing?
interview.answer: Discovery identifies current destinations or a stable service address; load balancing chooses how traffic is distributed among usable targets. Platforms may combine them.
interview.followUp: Who chooses the instance in your design?

interview.question: How do stale records affect recovery?
interview.answer: Cached addresses and long-lived connections can continue pointing at old instances. Use suitable lifetimes, retries and draining and test convergence.
interview.followUp: Does reducing TTL instantly move all clients?

quiz.question: A discovered service name proves:
options: A naming mechanism returned a destination, not that every call will succeed
quiz.explanation: Discovery does not replace health, network checks or authorization.

steps.title: Ask for a stable name
steps.detail: The caller requests the payment capability by service name instead of storing an individual pod address that may disappear during the next deployment.

steps.title: Maintain endpoints
steps.detail: The platform or registry tracks service destinations and readiness. Registration and removal need reliable ownership and observable convergence.

steps.title: Choose a destination
steps.detail: Client or server routing selects a usable endpoint. Discovery and load balancing cooperate, but they describe different responsibilities.

steps.title: Replace an instance
steps.detail: An old instance becomes unready and a replacement joins. Cached addresses and existing connections can outlive the registry update.

steps.title: Retry within a budget
steps.detail: A failed connection may use a safe bounded retry against current membership. Do not hide repeated errors with unlimited retries.

steps.title: Verify service identity
steps.detail: Knowing an address does not authorize a request. Validate the relevant identity, transport security and resource permissions at the appropriate boundaries.

title: Reverse proxy
simple: A reverse proxy receives requests on behalf of backend servers and forwards them. It can terminate TLS, route paths or hosts and manage forwarding behavior. It is different from a forward proxy used on behalf of clients.
analogy: A reception desk receives mail for several offices and forwards each envelope internally. Outside visitors know the public address rather than every room. The desk must preserve important information and must not believe a forged note saying that an envelope came from the principal.
why: SeatSpot can expose one HTTPS hostname while forwarding application and static paths to different backends. This central entry layer needs deliberate timeout, buffering and trusted-header behavior.
engineering: Decide where TLS terminates and whether backend connections also use TLS. Preserve/transform Host and forwarded headers deliberately. Backend code must trust identity/IP headers only from a known proxy chain.
Set request/body limits, connect/read timeouts and buffering behavior for the workload. A streaming response or WebSocket needs suitable handling rather than assuming ordinary buffered HTTP defaults.

A reverse proxy may also load balance or apply API policies. Avoid treating these roles as mutually exclusive products. Plan proxy redundancy and test backend failure and graceful connection draining.

worked.scenario: A browser uploads a large image through a proxy to the application.
worked.calculation: The application body limit does not help if the proxy rejects it first; conversely, a permissive proxy does not bypass the application validation. The smallest relevant limit wins.
worked.decision: Align intended limits and return understandable errors. For streaming, inspect buffering and timeouts along the full path.

implementation.explanation: A minimal local example, not complete production configuration. proxy_pass URI/trailing-slash behavior matters; configure TLS, trusted headers and workload-specific limits separately.

useCases: One public entry point for internal HTTP applications.
TLS termination, path routing and suitable buffering policies.
pitfalls: Trusting arbitrary forwarded-IP headers.
Breaking streams with inappropriate buffering/timeouts.
Assuming proxy and application limits are identical.

exercise.prompt: An API stream produces tokens but the browser sees them all at once. What might be happening?
hints: Check intermediary buffering as well as application flushing.
Observe timing at more than one boundary.
exercise.solution: A proxy/CDN may buffer the response. Verify streaming support, flush behavior, timeout and cache/compression policies across the actual path before changing application logic blindly.

interview.question: Reverse proxy versus forward proxy?
interview.answer: A reverse proxy represents servers to incoming clients. A forward proxy represents clients making outbound requests. Either can have additional security or caching roles.
interview.followUp: Where is the trust boundary for client identity?

interview.question: Why is the client IP difficult?
interview.answer: Multiple proxies can add or rewrite headers. Trust only headers supplied by verified infrastructure and define how the chain is parsed.
interview.followUp: What prevents a direct client from spoofing that header?

quiz.question: Forwarded identity headers should be:
options: Trusted only through a verified infrastructure boundary
quiz.explanation: Untrusted clients can forge ordinary HTTP headers.

steps.title: Receive the public request
steps.detail: The browser talks to one public address. The reverse proxy represents backend servers rather than acting as the browser own outbound proxy.

steps.title: Apply forwarding rules
steps.detail: Host and path rules select a backend. Request size, deadlines, TLS termination and supported protocols must fit the actual workload.

steps.title: Forward the request
steps.detail: API traffic reaches the API backend and asset traffic can reach another backend. A reverse proxy can also perform load-balancing duties.

steps.title: Preserve trusted context
steps.detail: Forward useful request context, but do not accept forged identity or client-IP headers from arbitrary clients as trusted facts.

steps.title: Handle streaming deliberately
steps.detail: Buffering and idle/read timeouts can change what a browser sees. Test streams and long-lived connections end to end instead of assuming default behavior fits.

steps.title: Protect the proxy tier
steps.detail: The public entry point needs its own capacity, redundancy and monitoring. Backend replicas do not help if the only proxy is unavailable.

title: DNS management
simple: DNS translates names into records such as addresses. Managing DNS includes authoritative records, TTL, delegation and safe changes. It is not an HTTP redirect and does not instantly move every existing connection.
analogy: A phone book maps a name to a number. People who wrote down yesterday number may keep using it until they check again. Changing the book cannot hang up every current call. DNS caches and existing network connections behave similarly.
why: SeatSpot changes an application endpoint or validates a domain. A safe release must account for record type, current TTL, certificate/host configuration and rollback rather than assuming Save means every user changed immediately.
engineering: Distinguish recursive resolvers from authoritative name servers. A/AAAA map names to IPv4/IPv6 addresses; CNAME aliases a name with DNS constraints; TXT stores verification or other text. An HTTP redirect is an application response after a connection is made.

TTL controls how long compliant caches can retain a record. Lowering TTL at change time does not erase copies cached under the previous higher TTL. Plan ahead and keep the old endpoint safe during migration.

Protect DNS access, validate delegation and keep rollback records. DNS health routing depends on detection and caching, so it is not instantaneous failover. Verify resolution from relevant resolvers and actual HTTP/TLS behavior.

worked.scenario: A record was cached at 10:00 with a 3,600 second TTL. You lower TTL at 10:10.
worked.calculation: That existing cache may retain the old answer until about 11:00. The new shorter TTL affects later fetched answers, not already cached copies.
worked.decision: Reduce TTL in advance when appropriate, prepare both endpoints and monitor the transition. Keep domain ownership, DNS and hosting configuration separate in your explanation.

implementation.code:
dig example.com A
dig example.com AAAA
dig example.com NS
dig example.com TXT
# Read-only examples; replace with a domain you manage.
implementation.explanation: These commands inspect records where dig is installed. They do not edit DNS, prove application health or configure a Vercel/Spaceship account.

useCases: Domain verification and hostname routing.
Planned endpoint migrations and controlled DNS failover.
pitfalls: Calling a CNAME an HTTP 301 redirect.
Expecting TTL changes to clear every resolver immediately.
Forgetting certificates, host routing and the old endpoint.

exercise.prompt: Why do two users reach different servers after a DNS update?
hints: Their resolvers may hold different cached answers.
Existing connections are separate from new lookups.
exercise.solution: Resolvers fetched answers at different times and may retain previous TTLs. Clients may also reuse existing connections. Inspect records and actual request routing before concluding the update failed.

interview.question: What happens when you type a hostname?
interview.answer: Describe resolver/cache lookup, authoritative resolution when needed, connection establishment and TLS/HTTP. DNS is one stage, not the whole request.
interview.followUp: Where can stale information remain?

interview.question: How do you prepare a DNS cutover?
interview.answer: Validate target/TLS, plan TTL ahead, keep overlap/rollback and measure both resolution and application behavior.
interview.followUp: What if the old TTL was one day?

quiz.question: Lowering TTL right now:
options: Affects future fetched records but not all existing caches instantly
quiz.explanation: Previously cached answers can remain valid according to their original lifetime.

steps.title: Look up the name
steps.detail: The browser or operating system asks a resolver for the hostname. Existing local or resolver caches may already contain an answer.

steps.title: Query authority if needed
steps.detail: A resolver without a usable cached answer follows DNS resolution to the authoritative records. Record type and delegation must be configured correctly.

steps.title: Use a cached answer
steps.detail: A client may connect to the old endpoint while its answer is still valid. Changing the authoritative record does not instantly erase that cached answer.

steps.title: Fetch the new answer
steps.detail: Later lookups can obtain the new destination. Clients and resolvers change at different times, so old and new endpoints may both receive traffic.

steps.title: Verify beyond DNS
steps.detail: The new address also needs the correct certificate, host routing and healthy application. Successful resolution alone does not prove the website works.

steps.title: Plan safe overlap
steps.detail: Keep a rollback path and an appropriate overlap interval. Lower TTL in advance when useful; do not expect a last-second TTL edit to end existing connections.

title: Disaster recovery
simple: Disaster recovery is a tested plan for restoring required service and data after a serious disruption. Define the acceptable recovery time and acceptable data-loss window, then prove your procedure can meet them.
analogy: A student keeps a second copy of schoolwork in another safe place and practises opening it on a different computer. Knowing a copy exists is not enough if it is unreadable, its password is lost or it takes days to find. Recovery is the complete ability to resume useful work.
why: SeatSpot needs a response to regional loss, accidental deletion or corruption. Application replicas alone do not restore deleted orders or missing secrets/configuration.
engineering: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the target time to restore required service; recovery point objective (RPO) is the acceptable data-loss window measured in time. State the business operation and how these targets are measured.

Choose backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby or an active multi-site design according to requirements and cost. Include infrastructure definitions, secrets recovery, dependencies, credentials, DNS, monitoring and people/runbooks, not just a database snapshot.

Perform restore drills in an isolated environment and validate actual data, integrity and application behavior. Replication can reproduce deletion/corruption, so backups and point-in-time recovery remain separate protections.

worked.scenario: The business requires an illustrative RTO of 60 minutes and RPO of 15 minutes. Backups run every hour.
worked.calculation: Hourly-only backups can leave nearly an hour of missing data, exceeding a 15-minute RPO. A 60-minute RTO also includes provisioning, restore, validation and traffic recovery, not just file download time.
worked.decision: Select a suitable backup/log capture strategy and rehearse the whole path. Targets are objectives; measured drill results establish whether the current plan meets them.

implementation.code:
Recovery drill checklist:
1. Isolate recovery environment
2. Restore infrastructure, secrets and data
3. Verify counts, integrity and critical workflows
4. Measure recovery time and lost-data window
5. Record gaps and retest
implementation.explanation: A non-destructive planning checklist, not instructions to restore over a live production database. Real recovery needs approved environment-specific procedures.

useCases: Regional/service loss and data corruption recovery.
Business continuity with measurable downtime/data-loss objectives.
pitfalls: Confusing an RPO objective with a guarantee.
Never testing a restore.
Keeping every backup in the same compromised failure boundary.

exercise.prompt: A restore finishes in 40 minutes but application validation and routing take another 35. Does it meet a 60-minute RTO?
hints: Measure usable service, not one step.
Include all recovery dependencies.
exercise.solution: No: the measured end-to-end recovery is 75 minutes. Improve or revise the plan based on business requirements and repeat the drill.

interview.question: How do you prove backups are useful?
interview.answer: Restore them in isolation, query and validate data, run critical workflows and measure the full recovery time and achievable data-loss window.
interview.followUp: Which credential or encryption key might prevent a restore?

interview.question: HA versus DR?
interview.answer: High availability addresses defined ongoing service failures; disaster recovery restores service/data after a larger disruption. Their scopes can overlap, but replicas do not replace a tested restore plan.
interview.followUp: What if accidental deletion replicates to every live copy?

quiz.question: RPO describes:
options: The time taken by DNS lookup
quiz.explanation: RTO concerns recovery duration; RPO concerns how far back recoverable data may be.

steps.title: Set recovery objectives
steps.detail: Define how long the required user operation may be unavailable and how much recent data loss is acceptable. These are explicit business objectives, not product defaults.

steps.title: Preserve recoverable state
steps.detail: Capture suitable backups and change logs with recoverable keys and configuration. Live replication alone may copy deletion or corruption to every current replica.

steps.title: Lose production
steps.detail: A serious failure interrupts the production environment. Recovery needs an environment, permissions and an executable runbook, not merely a promise that a backup exists.

steps.title: Restore in isolation
steps.detail: Rebuild required infrastructure and restore data in a safe environment. Include secrets, certificates, queues and other dependencies required for actual user workflows.

steps.title: Validate before routing
steps.detail: Query restored data and run correctness checks. A process reporting restore complete does not prove that bookings, ownership and payment reconciliation are usable.

steps.title: Measure and improve
steps.detail: Restore traffic safely and compare measured end-to-end recovery and data loss with the objectives. Record gaps, improve the runbook and repeat the drill.

title: Zero-downtime deployments
simple: A zero-downtime deployment aims to release a change without interrupting required user operations. Rolling or blue-green rollout helps, but database compatibility, readiness and connection draining are part of the design.
analogy: A school repairs one classroom while students use another ready room. Moving students before the new room has desks causes disruption. Throwing away the old room key before every class moves makes rollback difficult. Old and new arrangements must coexist safely during the transition.
why: SeatSpot must release a booking API while active users and old mobile clients remain. New code and old code may run simultaneously against the same data.
engineering: Rolling deployment gradually replaces replicas; blue-green prepares a separate version then switches traffic; canaries expose a limited audience first. Each approach has different capacity and rollback requirements.

Readiness should mean the instance can serve intended traffic, not merely that its process started. Drain in-flight requests, close long-lived connections deliberately and allow graceful shutdown. Available spare capacity must cover the rollout.

Use expand/contract schema changes: introduce a compatible representation, migrate/backfill safely, switch readers/writers and only later remove old structures. Rolling back code does not undo an irreversible data migration.

worked.scenario: Four replicas must remain available; one replacement is created before one old replica is removed.
worked.calculation: The rollout temporarily needs capacity for five. If no spare capacity exists, readiness and rollout policy can stall. This simple count excludes node limits and dependency capacity.
worked.decision: Test old/new coexistence and rollback with real requests. Treat zero downtime as a measured release goal, not an unconditional Kubernetes flag.

implementation.code:
# Deployment strategy fragment
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
    maxSurge: 1
# Also define readiness and graceful termination.
implementation.explanation: This fragment requires a complete Deployment and spare scheduling capacity. It does not guarantee database compatibility, successful probes or uninterrupted long-lived connections.

useCases: Releasing user-facing services with an availability objective.
Gradual validation and controlled rollback of compatible versions.
pitfalls: Marking a pod ready before initialization is complete.
Dropping a database column still read by the old version.
Assuming code rollback reverses data changes.

exercise.prompt: Version B renames a database field and Version A still runs. What safer migration sequence can you use?
hints: Make old and new versions compatible first.
Destructive cleanup belongs after migration and verification.
exercise.solution: Expand with the new field, implement compatible reads/writes, backfill and validate, switch traffic/readers, then contract only when old users are gone. Plan failure/rollback at each step.

interview.question: Why can rolling deployment still cause downtime?
interview.answer: Bad readiness, insufficient headroom, incompatible contracts/schema, connection interruption or a shared dependency can break users while replicas appear available.
interview.followUp: How do you test WebSockets or long-running jobs?

interview.question: Canary success metric?
interview.answer: Compare user-visible errors, latency and correctness with a control, watch dependency saturation and use explicit rollback criteria. Small samples can hide rare failures.
interview.followUp: Which operation would you validate for a ticket sale?

quiz.question: maxUnavailable: 0 guarantees:
options: A desired rollout availability constraint, not complete application correctness
quiz.explanation: Controller settings do not prove readiness, compatibility or dependency health.

steps.title: Serve the old version
steps.detail: Visitors use the existing version while the next release is prepared. Establish user-visible metrics and rollback conditions before shifting traffic.

steps.title: Start the replacement
steps.detail: Create new capacity without immediately removing all old instances. Download, initialization and dependency setup take time and need spare resources.

steps.title: Check readiness
steps.detail: The readiness gate verifies the instance can serve the intended request. A running process with missing dependencies should not receive normal traffic yet.

steps.title: Shift traffic gradually
steps.detail: Send a bounded share to the new version and drain old work deliberately. Monitor errors and latency for real user operations, not only process health.

steps.title: Keep data compatible
steps.detail: Both versions can access the database during rollout. Expand and migrate safely before removing fields or behavior the old version still needs.

steps.title: Validate rollback
steps.detail: Stop or reverse traffic movement if the release violates its criteria. Code rollback cannot magically reverse incompatible or destructive data changes.

title: Distributed tracing
simple: Distributed tracing follows one operation across multiple components using linked spans and propagated context. It helps locate time and errors, but traces are sampled evidence, not proof that every request behaved the same way.
analogy: A parcel carries a tracking number through several delivery centres. Each centre records when its part began and ended. You can find where this parcel waited. That does not mean every parcel took the same path, and missing a tracking scan does not prove the parcel disappeared.
why: SeatSpot checkout passes through gateway, booking, database and payment. One total latency number cannot show which hop waited or whether two operations ran in parallel.
engineering: A trace groups related spans; spans record operation timing, parent relationships and attributes. Propagate context across HTTP and messaging boundaries using compatible instrumentation. Broken context creates disconnected fragments.

Nested and parallel span durations must not be blindly added. Inspect the critical path and missing time. Sampling affects which requests are visible; pair traces with aggregated metrics and contextual logs.

Avoid secrets, payment data and unnecessary personal identifiers in span attributes. Bound high-cardinality fields and restrict observability access/retention. Instrumenting everything without a budget can add cost and overhead.

worked.scenario: Checkout has a 100 ms database call and a 300 ms provider call in parallel, plus about 40 ms sequential overhead.
worked.calculation: A simplified total is about 340 ms, not 440 ms. Actual scheduling, serialization and network effects require measured traces.
worked.decision: Investigate the critical path and compare slow traces with broader metrics. Do not optimize a fast database span just because it is easiest to see.

implementation.code:
trace: checkout
  gateway                 0–340 ms
    booking              10–330 ms
      database           20–120 ms
      payment            20–320 ms
# database/payment overlap; do not add them blindly.
implementation.explanation: Illustrative timing data, not production telemetry or benchmark results. A real trace also needs propagated identity, errors and instrumentation context.

useCases: Finding bottlenecks in distributed requests.
Correlating partial failures across service boundaries.
pitfalls: Adding parallel durations as if sequential.
Putting access tokens or card details in attributes.
Assuming sampled traces represent all traffic.

exercise.prompt: Two 200 ms spans run in parallel inside a 250 ms request. Is the request necessarily missing 150 ms?
hints: Draw the time intervals.
Parent and child durations overlap.
exercise.solution: No. Parallel spans overlap, so their sum can exceed wall-clock request duration. Inspect start/end times and the critical path before inferring missing time.

interview.question: Logs, metrics or traces?
interview.answer: Metrics show aggregate behavior, logs capture contextual records and traces link work across a request path. Use them together; no single signal answers every question.
interview.followUp: How do you find whether a slow sampled trace is common?

interview.question: What if a message starts a new trace?
interview.answer: Explain propagation and span links/asynchronous boundaries. A consumer may continue or link causal context depending on instrumentation and semantics.
interview.followUp: What sensitive attributes would you prohibit?

quiz.question: Two child spans overlap. Their durations:
options: Always add to the parent duration
Can sum to more than request wall-clock time
quiz.explanation: Parallel work and nested timing overlap; inspect the timeline.

steps.title: Start one operation
steps.detail: The gateway starts or receives trace context for checkout. Its span represents one part of the operation, not all system traffic.

steps.title: Propagate context
steps.detail: Booking receives compatible context and creates a related span. Without propagation, downstream records can appear as unrelated operations.

steps.title: Record parallel work
steps.detail: Database and payment calls run in parallel in this teaching example. Their intervals overlap, so adding both durations would overstate wall-clock time.

steps.title: Collect span evidence
steps.detail: Instrumentation exports spans to an observability backend. Export buffering, sampling and failures mean a trace view is not a complete audit of every request.

steps.title: Find the slow boundary
steps.detail: Compare the critical path, errors and dependency waits. Combine traces with aggregate metrics to determine whether the visible slow request reflects a widespread problem.

steps.title: Protect telemetry data
steps.detail: Do not attach secrets or unnecessary personal data to spans. Keep attribute cardinality, access, sampling and retention within a deliberate observability budget.

title: Network segmentation
simple: Network segmentation limits which systems may communicate across network boundaries. It reduces reachability and blast radius. It does not replace identity checks, encryption or resource-level authorization.
analogy: A school separates the public reception, classrooms and locked records room. A visitor can enter reception without getting a path to every room. A classroom door being reachable still does not authorize reading a student file. Network access and application permission remain different checks.
why: SeatSpot public web traffic should not directly reach the orders database or administrative services. Booking may need a narrow database connection while an unrelated image worker does not.
engineering: Map the required flows by source, destination, protocol and port. Apply least privilege and explicitly allow required DNS, monitoring and other dependencies. A deny rule that breaks name resolution can look like an application outage.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy needs a network implementation that enforces it. Ingress and egress isolation are separate; namespace and pod selectors have specific semantics. Test actual allowed and denied connections from the relevant workloads.

Segmentation can limit lateral movement, but compromised allowed callers still need authentication/authorization boundaries. Protect management access, credentials and encrypted transport separately, and observe unexpected denied flows.

worked.scenario: Only the booking workload should initiate the database application connection on its configured port.
worked.calculation: A rule allowing the whole namespace may expose more callers than intended; a narrower pod selector can express the required source if labels and enforcement are trustworthy.
worked.decision: Test a permitted booking connection and a denied unrelated-worker connection. Also verify DNS and any cross-namespace behavior in the actual cluster.

implementation.explanation: Example ingress policy within one namespace; it needs an enforcing network plugin and correct labels. It does not configure egress, TLS, database credentials or application ownership checks.

useCases: Restricting unnecessary internal reachability.
Separating public, service, data and management boundaries.
pitfalls: Assuming a policy object guarantees enforcement.
Blocking DNS or observability accidentally.
Using network reachability instead of authorization.

exercise.prompt: A pod has a NetworkPolicy but unwanted traffic still reaches it. What do you verify?
hints: Check the selected pods and applicable policy set.
Check whether the network implementation enforces the policy.
exercise.solution: Verify enforcement support, labels/selectors, namespace semantics, ingress/egress direction and other allowed rules. Test from the real source workload rather than only inspecting YAML.

interview.question: How would you design segmentation?
interview.answer: Inventory required flows, default-deny where appropriate, allow narrow dependencies, test both success and denial, and observe effects. Keep identity and application permissions separate.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid blocking DNS?

interview.question: Is a private subnet enough?
interview.answer: No. Routing and network placement are one boundary. Credentials, application authorization, transport protection and management controls still matter.
interview.followUp: What can a compromised allowed client still attempt?

quiz.question: NetworkPolicy enforcement requires:
options: A supporting network implementation and correct selectors/rules
quiz.explanation: Intent and actual enforced network behavior must be verified.

steps.title: Map required flows
steps.detail: The public client needs the web tier, which needs booking. Booking needs the database. Record required ports and dependencies before introducing isolation.

steps.title: Remove unnecessary paths
steps.detail: The unrelated worker has no business requirement to contact the orders database. Blocking that path reduces reachability and potential blast radius.

steps.title: Allow a narrow connection
steps.detail: Permit the actual booking workload to use the configured database port. Broad namespace-wide rules may allow more callers than intended.

steps.title: Verify enforcement
steps.detail: A policy object is only configuration intent. The cluster network implementation must support and enforce it, and selectors must match the intended workloads.

steps.title: Keep identity checks
steps.detail: An allowed TCP connection is not permission to read every order. Database credentials, encrypted transport and application ownership checks remain separate controls.

steps.title: Test both directions
steps.detail: Verify allowed traffic, denied traffic and necessary DNS/monitoring dependencies. Observe unexpected failures and refine the policy without silently opening everything.

title: Multi-region setup
simple: A multi-region design runs required components in more than one geographic region. It can support regional recovery or lower user latency, but distant data coordination adds latency, consistency and operational trade-offs.
analogy: A school keeps a working campus in another city. Classes can move after a local disaster, but both campuses must agree which student records are current. If both sell the last seat in the same bus independently, simply having two campuses creates a conflict instead of solving it.
why: SeatSpot might serve public catalog reads near users in two regions while keeping seat reservation ownership in one write region. Choosing active-active writes requires an explicit conflict/coordination strategy, not merely deploying the same containers twice.
engineering: Active-passive keeps one site serving while another can take over; active-active serves from multiple sites. These labels must be defined for each operation because reads and writes can have different topologies.

Synchronous cross-region coordination adds distance-dependent latency and can refuse work when required peers cannot communicate. Asynchronous replication allows lag and possible recent-data loss/conflicts after failure. During a partition, state the consistency/availability choice precisely rather than saying pick any two without conditions.

Plan routing, data placement, write fencing, regional dependency independence, failback and drills. A second region that depends on the first region secrets, database or control plane may not survive the failure you intended to tolerate.

worked.scenario: Two regions can both see one remaining seat while cross-region communication is interrupted.
worked.calculation: If both independently confirm the seat, availability was preserved but the uniqueness invariant was broken. Preventing that requires a single owner, coordinated decision or a product model that explicitly tolerates/reconciles conflict.
worked.decision: Keep authoritative seat allocation under a clear ownership/consistency rule. Use regional catalog caches separately and test failover and failback with realistic lag.

implementation.code:
Public catalog: regional reads with bounded staleness
Seat allocation: one authoritative owner per seat
Failover: promote only after fencing old writer
Recovery: reconcile lag, route safely, test failback
implementation.explanation: A conceptual topology, not an automatic cloud failover script. The correct design depends on business invariants, supported storage guarantees and measured recovery requirements.

useCases: Regional disaster recovery with defined objectives.
Geographically distributed users with explicit data-locality/consistency needs.
pitfalls: Calling two deployments an independent multi-region service.
Ignoring conflicting writes and fencing.
Promising zero latency or zero data loss without a supported guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Both regions can independently book the last seat during a partition. What requirement is missing?
hints: Name the invariant first.
Decide who is allowed to confirm a write.
exercise.solution: There is no safe authoritative allocation/coordination rule for the uniqueness requirement. Define ownership, fencing and the partition policy; refuse or defer some writes if necessary rather than double-sell.

interview.question: How would you choose active-passive versus active-active?
interview.answer: Start with regional failure, latency, data-loss and consistency requirements for each operation. Compare operating cost, recovery evidence and write conflict handling.
interview.followUp: Can catalog reads and seat writes use different models?

interview.question: What makes failback hard?
interview.answer: Data may diverge, clients may keep old routes and in-flight work may exist in both sites. Reconcile ownership/state and drain safely before routing back.
interview.followUp: How do you prove the old writer cannot accept new writes?

quiz.question: During a network partition, confirming the same last seat independently in both regions can:
quiz.explanation: Write ownership and coordination are business correctness decisions, not consequences of adding a region.

steps.title: Define the regional goal
steps.detail: Decide whether another region is for disaster recovery, nearby reads or active writes. Each operation can have different latency, availability and consistency requirements.

steps.title: Copy suitable state
steps.detail: Region A sends changes toward Region B. Asynchronous copying can lag; synchronous coordination adds waiting and depends on the communication path.

steps.title: Lose the connection
steps.detail: The regions cannot communicate. Allowing both to confirm the same last seat independently can violate correctness even though both applications are running.

steps.title: Fence and promote
steps.detail: A safe failover establishes which writer owns new decisions and prevents the old writer from conflicting. Routing alone does not settle database ownership.

steps.title: Route and validate
steps.detail: Direct eligible traffic to the recovery region and validate the actual booking workflow. Its capacity, credentials and dependencies must work independently enough for the failure scenario.

steps.title: Plan reconciliation and failback
steps.detail: After recovery, reconcile lag and in-flight work before moving ownership back. Test both failover and failback instead of treating the first traffic switch as the whole plan.
